subject: Marketplace vs Direct Agreement — cost, billing, and support tradeoffs
messages:
From: Samir Patel <sam@finpulse.ai>
To: Priya Natarajan <priya@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: procurement@finpulse.ai
Date: 2027-04-07T08:12:00-07:00
Subject: Questions on buying via Marketplace vs Direct Agreement

Hi Priya,

We're starting the procurement review for an initial pilot of Redwood across two teams (ML infra + product). Procurement sent a short list of questions and asked I confirm high-level differences between buying through AWS/Azure/GCP marketplaces versus a direct Redwood contract (MSA + PO). Can you confirm the practical differences on the following?

1) Invoicing & PO flow — our finance team requires a vendor invoice and PO-based terms; do marketplace purchases support PO-to-invoice matching or do we need a private offer/direct invoice?
2) Billing cadence & credits — if we start with free/credit pilot credits, how are those represented on marketplace bills vs direct invoices?
3) Seller-of-record & tax/VAT — is Redwood the seller-of-record on each cloud marketplace, and does that change tax treatment?
4) Support & SLA entitlements — are production SLAs (uptime, latency targets, support response) available if we buy via marketplace, or is that only in a direct enterprise agreement?
5) Co-sell credits & partner incentives — does choosing marketplace vs direct change co-sell credits for any AWS/Azure partner programs?
6) Timeline — how long does it typically take to get a private offer or vendor invoice route in our experience (we're on a ~2 week procurement window)?

If it's easier, we can hop on a quick 20-minute call today — our procurement lead (procurement@finpulse.ai) is on the thread.

Thanks,
Samir
Samir Patel
Head of Platform
FinPulse Analytics

From: Priya Natarajan <priya@redwoodinference.com>

Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwoodinference.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwoodinference.com>

Subject: Re: Questions on buying via Marketplace vs Direct Agreement

Hi Samir — thanks for the clear list. I put together the short answers below and attached a one-page checklist that procurement often finds useful. If helpful I'll book a 20-min sync this afternoon with Ben (handling co-sell) and Lauren (billing/contracts).

Quick answers (high-level):
- Invoicing & PO flow: Marketplaces typically use the cloud vendor as the seller-of-record (SoR). That means your PO is to AWS/Azure/GCP and the invoice will come from them. If your finance team requires a vendor invoice directly from Redwood (company name on invoice + specific PO matching), we usually use a private offer / directed invoice route (private offer on AWS, CSP private billing on Azure, or direct invoice on GCP).
- Billing cadence & credits: Marketplace credits are applied on the cloud vendor bill and show up as line items; private offers/direct invoices allow us to reflect promotional credits as discounts/credits on Redwood's invoice which some customers prefer for internal cost tracking.
- Seller-of-record & tax: Yes, most cloud marketplaces list the cloud vendor as SoR which changes VAT/tax handling in some jurisdictions. Direct contracts keep Redwood as SoR and simplify vendor tax paperwork for finance teams that need it.
- Support & SLA: Basic support tiers are available if you buy from marketplace, but enterprise SLAs (SLA-backed latency/uptime targets, named support pathways, on-call escalation) are contract items we include in direct enterprise agreements. We can attach SLA addenda to a private offer as well — Ben can expand.
- Co-sell credits: Buying through marketplace can still enable partner incentives but the timing and eligibility differ by program — private offers that go through co-sell channels often unlock clearer credits and faster partner compensation.
- Timeline: For straightforward private offers we typically see 3–10 business days (depends on cloud partner PO processing). Marketplace listing changes are slower (weeks) if a new SKU/listing is required.

Attachments: Redwood_Marketplace_vs_Direct_Checklist.pdf (one-pager), AWS_Private_Offer_Timeline.xlsx

Next steps: If the procurement team needs Redwood to appear as vendor on the invoice, we should start the private-offer path now. Ben/Lauren: can you confirm typical SLAs and whether we need any paperwork from FinPulse to initiate the private offer?

Best,

Samir — quick note to add detail on co-sell and SLAs.

- Co-sell: For AWS/Marketplace private offers, we generally coordinate with the partner team to register the opportunity and file the co-sell paperwork. That registration usually needs an estimate of ARR/commit and expected go-live. When done early, it preserves co-sell credits for the partner and speeds up certain approvals.
- SLAs & support: We can include an SLA attachment in a direct agreement that defines performance targets (p99 latency, regional availability SLOs) and a two-tier escalation path (customer success -> platform incident -> engineering on-call). If you buy on marketplace without a private offer, you still get standard support but not the SLA guarantees in the same way.
- Timeline & operational ask: To start a private offer we need: (1) billing contact + PO term, (2) tax/VAT entity info, (3) expected pilot footprint (avg concurrent requests / peak token throughput). With those, we open the private-offer request; AWS processing is usually 3–7 business days from submission.

Thanks Priya and Ben — that's very helpful. Procurement confirms that their payment process requires a vendor invoice (Redwood name on the invoice) and PO-to-invoice matching, so we'd prefer the private-offer / direct-invoice route even if it adds a few days.

Action items from our side:
- I'll send finance the tax entity details and draft PO (procurement@finpulse.ai).
- Can Redwood share a draft quote / SOW that we can attach to the PO? If possible, a simple quote with line items for pilot usage and an optional expansion SKU would be great.

We're flexible on a short call — if you want to schedule 10–15 minutes to confirm the three data points Ben listed, afternoon Pacific works for us.

Appreciate the quick turnaround.
Samir
